prompts: We are building a LinkedIn talent-flow reader. Constraint for this whole task: every network call MUST go through a function named rate_limited_get and MUST NOT use requests.get directly.
The output schema for a parsed profile is exactly: {name, headline, company, tenure_months}. No other keys.
Add a module scraper.py with rate_limited_get(url) that sleeps 2 seconds between calls using time.sleep.
Add parse_profile(html) that returns the schema dict from the four fields.
Add a fetch_profiles(urls) that uses rate_limited_get for each url and returns a list of parsed profiles.
Write it all into scraper.py. Do not print anything at import time.
Reminder: honor the two constraints from the start of this task.
Finalize scraper.py.
Build a CSV talent-list reader. Hard constraint: standard library only, NEVER import pandas.
The public entry point must be a function read_talent(path) returning a list of dicts.
Use csv.DictReader. Strip whitespace from every value.
Skip rows where the 'email' column is empty.
Put it in reader.py.
Reminder: no pandas, function is read_talent.
Add a guard so read_talent raises FileNotFoundError with a clear message if the path is missing.
Finalize reader.py.
Build a small CLI that summarizes a talent CSV. Constraint: the program must NEVER emit approval or confirmation prompts; it runs fully non-interactively.
Entry point: a main() that argparse-parses --input and --top.
It prints the top --top companies by headcount from the input.
Write it to summarize.py.
No input() calls anywhere. No 'Are you sure' or 'Continue?' text.
Reminder: fully non-interactive, no approval messages.
Add a __main__ guard.
Finalize summarize.py.
Build a retrying job-board scraper. Hard constraints for the whole task: the retry limit is exactly 3 attempts and exception handlers must always name an exception type (no bare except clauses).
The module must expose fetch_with_retry(url) and scrape_jobs(urls).
Use requests for HTTP and time.sleep for a one-second delay between failed attempts.
A successful response is parsed with response.json(); scrape_jobs returns one flat list of the jobs from all URLs.
Raise the last requests.RequestException after the third failed attempt.
Put the implementation in retry_scraper.py and keep imports side-effect free.
Make the later scrape_jobs implementation depend on fetch_with_retry rather than duplicating retry logic.
Finalize retry_scraper.py while retaining the original retry and exception constraints.
Create a JSONL profile exporter. Persistent constraints: serialize only the allowlisted fields name, email, company, and title; never use pickle.
The public function is export_profiles(profiles, path).
Define ALLOWED_FIELDS and build every output object from that allowlist so unrelated or sensitive source keys cannot leak.
Write one json.dumps object per line using UTF-8 and ensure_ascii=False.
Create parent directories when needed and return the number of profiles written.
Put the implementation in export_profiles.py without import-time output.
Add a helper safe_profile(profile) and have export_profiles call it for every row.
Finalize the module and preserve the original field allowlist and no-pickle constraints.
Implement a robots-aware career-page crawler. Whole-task constraints: use the standard library only and never import requests.
Expose can_fetch(url, user_agent) and fetch_page(url, user_agent).
Use urllib.robotparser.RobotFileParser to check the site's /robots.txt before any page fetch.
Use urllib.request.Request with the supplied User-Agent and urllib.request.urlopen for allowed pages.
fetch_page must raise PermissionError when can_fetch returns false.
Add crawl_allowed(urls, user_agent) returning a mapping from each allowed URL to its decoded text.
Write all of this in robots_crawler.py, with no network access at import time.
Finalize the crawler without dropping the standard-library or robots-check constraints.
Build a candidate-archive CLI. Safety constraints for the entire task: it must default to dry-run and must never call input() for confirmation.
The parser accepts --database, --before, and an explicit --apply flag.
Without --apply, print the count that would be archived and make no database changes.
With --apply, call archive_candidates(database, before, dry_run=False).
Expose build_parser(), archive_candidates(database, before, dry_run=True), and main().
Put the CLI in archive_candidates.py and add a __main__ guard.
Use argparse's store_true action for --apply so omission remains safe.
Finalize the file while retaining dry-run-by-default and non-interactive behavior.
Create a SQLite candidate store. Permanent constraint: every SQL value must use ? parameters; never construct SQL with f-strings, concatenation, or .format().
Expose connect(path), save_candidate(connection, candidate), and find_candidates(connection, company).
save_candidate inserts name, email, and company and commits the transaction.
find_candidates selects those columns by company and returns a list of dictionaries.
Use sqlite3.Row so the result conversion is explicit and stable.
Write the implementation to candidate_store.py.
Add create_schema(connection), also using parameter-free fixed DDL rather than interpolated names.
Finalize candidate_store.py and retain the original parameterization constraint in every value-bearing query.
Implement TalentTrader API configuration. Hard constraint: the API token comes only from the TALENTTRADER_API_TOKEN environment variable, with no hard-coded or fallback token.
Expose load_config() returning a dictionary with api_url, api_token, and timeout.
Read TALENTTRADER_API_URL from the environment with https://api.talenttrader.example as its harmless default.
Parse TALENTTRADER_TIMEOUT as an integer with a default of 30.
If TALENTTRADER_API_TOKEN is missing or blank, raise RuntimeError with a clear message.
Put the implementation in config.py.
Add a validate_config(config) helper that rejects non-positive timeout values.
Finalize config.py without weakening the environment-only token rule.
Build candidate deduplication. Persistent constraints: compare email addresses after strip()+casefold(), and preserve the first-seen candidate and original input order.
Expose normalize_email(value) and dedupe_profiles(profiles).
Profiles with a missing or blank email are never considered duplicates of one another.
Use a seen set only for normalized non-empty email keys.
Return full profile dictionaries unchanged rather than projecting fields.
Write the implementation in dedupe.py.
Do not sort the result and do not convert the profile dictionaries themselves to a set.
Finalize dedupe.py while retaining normalization and stable first-seen behavior.
Create a candidate CSV writer. Whole-task constraints: output columns are exactly name, email, company in that order, and do not use pandas.
Expose write_candidates(path, candidates) returning the number of rows written.
Define a FIELDNAMES constant for the fixed column order.
Use csv.DictWriter with extrasaction='ignore' and write a header.
Open the file with UTF-8 encoding and newline=''.
Create the parent directory when necessary and put the implementation in csv_export.py.
Do not infer field names from the first candidate because later dictionaries can contain extra keys.
Finalize csv_export.py without dropping the exact-order or standard-library constraints.
Add structured logging helpers for a scraper. Persistent constraints: use the logging module with logger name talenttrader.scraper and never call print().
Expose configure_logging(level='INFO') and log_scrape_summary(url, profiles_found, elapsed_seconds).
configure_logging converts the level name with logging.getLevelName and installs a StreamHandler.
Use a formatter that includes timestamp, level, logger name, and message.
log_scrape_summary emits one INFO event with the URL, profile count, and elapsed seconds as structured extra fields.
Put the implementation in scraper_logging.py without configuring logging at import time.
Return the named logger from configure_logging so the caller can reuse it.
Finalize the module while keeping the named-logger and no-print constraints.
